The essential grievance of the Petitioner is as to the payment of lower amount of compensation for the land he lost in the KIADB acquisition.

Learned counsel for the Petitioner vehemently argues that his client being a nonagenarian, inadvertently accepted the award amount in a sum of Rs.4,76,46,008/- excluding the tax component of Rs.52,94,001/- and therefore, the award should be set at naught to re-determine the same at a much higher value.
Compensation.

He draws attention of the Court to several paragraphs of One Man Committee Report on the basis of which the subject determination was made, wrongly in the opinion of the counsel.
2.
After service of notice, the State has entered appearance through its AGA; the KIADB has entered its appearance through its Senior Panel Counsel and BMRCL is represented by its Senior Panel Advocate.
They have filed the Statement of Objections opposing the Petition.

All they make submission in justification of what has been paid as the compensation and ask the Court to dismiss C N Srinivasa Rao vs State Of Karnataka on 13 March, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/184148444/
2 the Petition on certain grounds which will be discussed in due course.

sentences.text:
3. Having heard the learned counsel for the parties and having perused the Petition Papers, this Court declines indulgence in the matter for the following reasons:
(a) Land of the Petitioner has been acquired under the provisions of the Karnataka Industrial Areas Development Act, 1966 and payment of compensation in terms of the award in a sum mentioned hereinabove has been made to him, is not in dispute.
Petitioner has accepted the offer of award amount and acknowledged the receipt thereof, is vouched by records.
In fact, that is not disputed at all.

Award of the Land Acquisition Officer is in the nature of an offer and the land loser has an option either to accept it unconditionally or with reservation so that he can seek higher compensation than awarded by seeking reference u/s 18 of the erstwhile Land Acquisition Act, 1894 or under such other law.

Once the award amount has been accepted without raising even a little finger, it is not open to the awardee to lay a challenge to the determination of the award subject to all just exceptions into which argued case of the Petitioner does not fit.

(b) The vehement submission of learned counsel for the Petitioner that his client being a 92 year old person, could not ascertain the pit falls in the determination of the award amount by way of compensation and therefore, he is entitled to seek re-determination thereof, is bit difficult to countenance.
May be that the Petitioner is as aged as is stated.

He is admittedly a businessman and no where in the petition or in the correspondence with the Respondents, he has mentioned anything about his disability that came in the way of ascertaining the argued infirmities in determining the compensation.
Had he been a peasant or a labourer, such a contention could have been arguably countenanced, is beside the point.
(c) The learned Advocates appearing for the Respondents have filed a wealth of material justifying rejection of the claim.

In the BMRCL's Statement of Objections dated 22.03.2016, Annexure-R1 happens to be the acknowledgement given by the Petitioner himself about the receipt of compensation after excluding the income tax component.
No reservation is mentioned in that.
Annexure-R3 happens to be the agreement drawn on a non-judicial stamp paper of Rs.100/-.
It mentions about the property, acquisition and specifically about the compensation amount fixed at Rs.4,76,46,008/-.
Each of the pages is signed both by the Petitioner and the Special Land Acquisition Officer.
There is not even a whisper about any objection or reservation as to the determination of the amount or the principles on which such determination is made.

Annexure-R4 is another non-judicial stamp paper of Rs.100/-
which specifically mentions about the acceptance of the compensation specified in the very same sum.

The first condition stipulated therein reads: "1.  a jg Pj  AiiAiP z Ug Mgvg."

sentences.text: The argument of Petitioner's counsel that it only bars his client from knocking at the doors of Civil Court by filing a suit and not the presentation of the Writ Petition, is too farfetched.
Such stipulations cannot be read as Euclid's theorem.

While construing the conditions of the kind,
common sense cannot be kept in cold storage, to say the least.
Thus, once the right to litigate over the determination of compensation is given up, a land owner cannot turn around and contend to the contrary.

(d) The vehement submission of learned counsel for the Petitioner that the said determination of compensation has been done to the disadvantage of his client by acting upon a One Man Committee Report and that the Committee had done its work without notice to his client and therefore,
re-determination of compensation is warranted, cannot be agreed to.
A perusal of the Committee Report does not show any infirmity in working out the parameters for determining the compensation.
It is not that the Committee Report has been straight away accepted by the SLAO while framing the award, as a gospel truth.

The same has been duly examined and only thereafter,
the determination of compensation has been done keeping in view all the parameters prescribed by law.
The argument of violation of principles of natural justice is more often made than established by cogent evidentiary material.

Not only the Petitioner should say that he was not heard in the matter, but demonstrate that such a hearing would have changed the outcome vide S.L.KAPOOR vs.
JAGMOHAN, AIR 1981 SC 136.
The violation of principles of natural justice cannot be ritualistically chanted as mantra, our system having moved from farm to substance after the Constitution has been enacted.

In the above circumstances, Writ Petition being devoid of merits, is liable to be dismissed &
accordingly, it is, costs having been reluctantly made easy.

Sd/-
